title: Paint a Room
summary: Paint a {{a.len}} x {{a.wid}} ft room: {{a.ceiling==='yes'?'ceiling, ':''}}walls{{a.trim==='yes'?' and trim':''}}, with clean lines, an even finish and the right amount of paint.
safety: In homes built before 1978, test for lead before sanding or scraping. Keep the room ventilated. Use a ladder you can stand on without stretching, never the top step. Wear glasses when painting overhead.
pro: you find lead paint you need to disturb, peeling paint over large areas, water damage or mold, or very high ceilings and stairwells that need scaffolding.

questions.label: Coverage on the can
questions.hint: Usually 350 to 400. Use the low number.

calcNote: Walls subtract about 21 sq ft per door and 15 per window. Coverage is {{a.cover}} sq ft per gallon per coat; textured walls and big color changes use more.

tools.w: Interior latex (acrylic). Eggshell or satin cleans easier than flat.
Flat paint hides ceiling flaws and reduces glare.
Hard and washable for trim and doors.

tools.n: Primer {{a.prime==='full'?'(ask for it tinted toward the new color)':'(stain-blocking for stains)'}}
tools.w: Seals patches and stains, and helps cover a big color change.
Cuts clean lines at corners, ceilings and trim.
One cover per color is easiest.
Rolls ceilings and tall walls without a ladder.

tools.n: Roller tray or 5-gallon bucket with grid, and liners
tools.w: Loads the roller evenly.
Easier to hold than a can when cutting in from a ladder.
Safe reach for cutting in at the ceiling.

tools.n: Canvas drop cloths and plastic sheeting
tools.w: Canvas doesn't get slippery; plastic covers furniture.
Optional edge protection for trim and ceilings.

tools.n: Lightweight spackle and a putty knife
tools.w: Fills nail holes and dings.
Smooths patches and scuffs glossy trim.
Removes grease and grime so paint sticks.

tools.n: Paintable acrylic latex caulk + caulk gun
tools.w: Fills gaps between trim and wall.
Removes outlet covers and switch plates.
Checks old paint before you sand or scrape.

tools.n: Safety glasses, gloves, N95 mask for sanding
tools.w: Protects eyes when painting overhead and lungs when sanding.
Cleanup and wiping drips.

steps.idea: Homes built before 1978 may have lead paint under the newer layers. Sanding or scraping it makes toxic dust.
steps.stop: If the test shows lead, don't dry-sand, scrape, or heat-strip. Keep kids and pregnant people out, and hire an EPA RRP-certified painter for prep, or follow lead-safe practices for minor work.
steps.b:
1. Pick spots you'll sand or scrape: window sills, door frames, baseboards, and chipped areas.
  2. Cut a small notch through all paint layers with a utility knife.
  3. Rub the test swab on the notch as the kit's instructions say.
  4. Read the color. Red or pink usually means lead.
  5. Painting over intact, unsanded lead paint is generally OK; the danger is dust and chips.
faq: The test is negative. Am I done?
Home kits can miss low levels. If you're unsure, a certified inspector can test with an XRF gun.

steps.t: Choose paint and sheen, and buy supplies
steps.idea: The right sheen for each surface and enough paint from one batch avoids mismatched color.
steps.b:
1. Pick the sheen for each surface (chart). Typical: flat ceiling, {{a.wallSheen}} walls, semi-gloss trim.
  2. Buy {{c.wallGal}} gal of wall paint{{a.ceiling==='yes'?', '+c.ceilGal+' gal of ceiling paint':''}}{{a.trim==='yes'?', and '+(c.trimQt>3?'1 gal':c.trimQt+' qt')+' of trim paint':''}}.
  3. If you need 4 or more gallons of one color, a 5-gallon bucket is often cheaper.
  4. Ask the store to shake every can. Buy it all at once; mix cans of the same color in a bucket ("box" them) so the color is even.
  5. Choose a roller nap for your wall texture: {{a.texture==='smooth'?'3/8"':a.texture==='light'?'1/2"':'3/4"'}}.
faq: Do I need expensive paint?
Mid-range or better paint covers in fewer coats and washes better. Very cheap paint often needs an extra coat.
Paint and primer in one?
Fine over clean, sound, painted walls of a similar color. Use separate primer on patches, stains and bare drywall.

steps.t: Empty the room and cover the floor
steps.idea: Space to work and covered floors save hours of cleanup.
steps.b:
1. Move small furniture out. Push big pieces to the center, at least 3 ft from walls, and cover with plastic.
  2. Take pictures and nails off the walls (leave nails where art goes back, or mark spots).
  3. Unscrew outlet covers and switch plates. Put screws in a bag taped to each plate.
  4. Lay canvas drop cloths along every wall, tight to the baseboard.
  5. Take down curtain rods, and loosen light fixture canopies if you're painting the ceiling.
faq: Do I need to turn off the power to remove plates?
No, just don't touch anything inside the box. Cover openings with painter's tape so paint doesn't get in.

steps.idea: Paint shows every hole, so fill them first. Big holes need a real patch.
steps.b:
1. Fill nail holes and dings with lightweight spackle and a putty knife.
  2. Scrape a little over the hole, then wipe flat with the knife.
  3. Larger holes, cracks, nail pops or water stains: see the Drywall Repair guide.
  4. Let it dry, then sand flush with a fine sanding sponge.
  5. Mark each patch with a light pencil circle so you remember to prime it.

steps.idea: Paint doesn't stick well to grease, dust or soap film.
steps.b:
1. Vacuum or dust the walls and baseboards, top to bottom.
  2. Mix TSP substitute with water as the label says.
  3. Wash greasy areas (kitchens, around switches) with a sponge.
  4. Rinse with clean water and a second sponge.
  5. Let walls dry, about an hour.
faq: There's mildew in the bathroom.
Clean it with a mildew cleaner, rinse and dry it before painting. Use a bath paint with mildewcide.

steps.idea: A thin bead of caulk closes the cracks where trim meets wall, so the paint line looks straight.
steps.b:
1. Cut the caulk tip at an angle, with a small hole (1/8").
  2. Push the gun along the gap at a steady speed.
  3. Smooth the bead with a damp finger and wipe your finger on a rag often.
  4. Wipe off extra with a damp rag right away.
  5. Let it dry for the time on the tube before painting.

steps.idea: New paint grips a dull surface. Glossy trim needs a light scuff.
steps.stop: Old trim in a pre-1978 home may have lead paint. Test before sanding.
steps.b:
1. Test the old paint: rub a spot with rubbing alcohol on a rag. If paint comes off, it's latex. If not, it's probably oil.
  2. Lightly sand all glossy trim with a fine sanding sponge until the shine is gone. Don't sand to bare wood.
  3. Wipe the dust off with a damp rag.
  4. Oil-based trim? Use a bonding primer before latex paint, or the new paint can peel.

steps.idea: Primer seals patches, blocks stains, and helps a new color cover.
steps.b:
1. Prime every spackle patch and drywall repair.
  2. Prime stains (water, smoke, marker) with a stain-blocking primer.
  3. {{a.prime==='full'?'Big color change or new drywall: prime the whole wall. Ask the store to tint the primer toward your new color.':'Spot priming only: feather the edges so no ridge shows.'}}
  4. Let it dry fully.
faq: Do I need primer to go from dark to light?
It helps a lot. A tinted primer coat usually saves a third coat of paint.

steps.idea: Tape protects trim and ceilings if your brush hand isn't steady yet.
steps.b:
1. Run tape along the edges you want to protect: tops of baseboards, door and window casing{{a.ceiling==='yes'?'':', and the ceiling edge'}}.
  2. Tear it in 2 to 3 ft pieces; long pieces stretch and wander.
  3. Press the edge down firmly with a putty knife so paint can't creep under.
  4. Don't tape over fresh paint or caulk until it's dry.

steps.idea: Brush a band around the edges of the ceiling where the roller can't reach.
steps.b:
1. Pour 1" to 2" of paint into a paint cup.
  2. Dip the brush 1/3 of the way in. Tap both sides on the cup; don't wipe.
  3. Brush a 2" to 3" band around the ceiling edges and around light fixtures.
  4. Let ceiling paint go onto the wall slightly. Walls get painted after.
  5. Move the ladder often. Don't stretch to reach.

steps.idea: Roll while the cut-in band is still wet, working across the room in strips.
steps.b:
1. Load the roller in the tray: roll it into the paint, then on the ridges until even.
  2. Start in a corner. Roll strips about 3 ft wide across the short direction of the room.
  3. Roll right up to the cut-in band and overlap it.
  4. Overlap each strip into the last one while it's wet.
  5. Finish each strip with light passes all in one direction.
faq: I see lines when it dries.
Usually a dry roller or uneven pressure. A second coat in the opposite direction usually fixes it.

steps.idea: A second coat hides roller marks and evens out the color.
steps.b:
1. Wait until the first coat's recoat time on the can has passed.
  2. Cut in again, then roll in the other direction from the first coat.
  3. Check from different angles with the light on.
  4. Let it dry before cutting in the walls.

steps.idea: Brush the corners and edges, one wall at a time, so you can roll while it's still wet.
steps.b:
1. Box the paint: pour all cans of the same color into a 5-gallon bucket and stir.
  2. Start at the top corner of one wall. Brush a 2" to 3" band along the ceiling line{{a.ceiling==='yes'?' (the ceiling paint should be dry)':''}}, inside corners, and around trim, outlets and switches.
  3. For a straight ceiling line: start the stroke 1/2" below the line, then press gently and slide so the bristles fan up to the line.
  4. Cut in only one or two walls at a time, then roll them before the band dries.
faq: I got paint on the ceiling.
Wipe it right away with a damp rag wrapped on a putty knife. Dried? Touch up with ceiling paint later.

steps.idea: Roll each wall corner to corner without stopping, overlapping into wet paint.
steps.b:
1. Load the roller evenly; it should be full but not dripping.
  2. Start about a roller width from a corner. Roll a W about 3 ft tall.
  3. Fill in the W without lifting the roller.
  4. Finish the section with light straight passes top to bottom.
  5. Move over and roll the next section back into the wet edge of the last.
  6. Keep rolling over the cut-in band so brush and roller textures match.
faq: The paint looks patchy when wet.
That's normal for one coat, especially with a color change. Judge it when dry, and after the second coat.

steps.idea: The second coat gives an even color and sheen.
steps.b:
1. Wait for the recoat time on the can, often 2 to 4 hours. Cool or humid rooms take longer.
  2. Cut in again, then roll exactly as before.
  3. Look along each wall with the light from the side for thin spots or drips.
  4. Fix drips while wet by rolling them out; if dried, sand smooth and touch up later.

steps.idea: Trim goes last because it's easier to cut a straight line onto trim than onto walls.
steps.b:
1. Let the walls dry. Tape the wall above the baseboards if you like.
  2. Start high: window casing, then door casing and doors, then baseboards last.
  3. Load the brush lightly. Brush along the length of each piece in long strokes.
  4. Finish each section with one light stroke end to end ("tipping off") to level the brush marks.
  5. Check for drips at corners and bottom edges after 5 minutes and brush them out.
  6. Second coat after the recoat time.
faq: Brush marks show in semi-gloss.
Use thinner coats and a good brush, and don't go back over paint that has started to dry. A paint conditioner (extender) helps it level.

steps.idea: Remove tape soon after the final coat, before the paint fully hardens.
steps.b:
1. Wait until the last coat is dry to the touch, usually 1 to 2 hours.
  2. Pull the tape back over itself at about 45 degrees, slowly.
  3. If paint starts to tear, score the edge with a sharp utility knife and keep pulling.
  4. Touch up any bleed with a small brush.

steps.idea: Clean tools last for years. Leftover paint is for touch-ups, not the drain.
steps.b:
1. Scrape extra paint from the roller and brush back into the can.
  2. Latex paint: wash brushes and rollers with warm, soapy water until it runs clear. Comb the bristles straight and hang to dry.
  3. Never pour paint down a sink, toilet or storm drain. If you're on a septic system, check before rinsing paint in a sink.
  4. Close cans tightly: lay plastic wrap over the opening and tap the lid down with a block.
  5. Label each can with the room and date. Store where it won't freeze.
  6. Get rid of unwanted paint the way your area allows: dry out small amounts with cat litter or hardener, or take it to a paint recycling or hazardous waste drop-off.
faq: What about oil-based paint?
Clean it with mineral spirits, never water. Lay used rags flat outdoors to dry, or put them in a sealed metal can with water: oily rags can catch fire on their own.

steps.t: Put the room back and touch up
steps.idea: Give paint a day before putting things against it, and touch up small spots with the same paint.
steps.b:
1. Reinstall outlet covers and switch plates once the paint is dry.
  2. Wait at least a day before pushing furniture against walls; paint stays soft for weeks.
  3. Look the room over in daylight. Circle spots with painter's tape.
  4. Touch up with a small brush and the same can, feathering the edges.
  5. Big touch-ups show? Repaint that wall corner to corner.

days.wait: Recoat time on the can, often 2 to 4 hours

brushHelp.b:
1. Dip the bristles 1/3 to 1/2 of their length.
  2. Tap each side against the inside of the cup. Don't scrape it off.
  3. Hold the brush by the ferrule (metal band) like a pencil.
  4. Lay paint down with the first strokes, then smooth with light, long strokes.
  5. Reload before the brush runs dry; dry brushing leaves streaks.

rollHelp.b:
1. Dampen a new cover with water for latex paint and spin it nearly dry.
  2. Roll into the deep end of the tray, then back and forth on the ridges.
  3. The cover should be evenly full, not dripping.
  4. Let the roller do the work: light, steady pressure.
  5. Reload often. A dry roller leaves thin, patchy paint.

sheen.cap: Shinier paint wipes clean but shows every bump and patch. Flatter paint hides them.

cutin.cap: Hold the brush like a pencil, narrow edge toward the line, and let the bristles push a thin bead of paint into the corner.

wroll.title: Roll a W pattern
wroll.cap: The W spreads the paint out evenly. Finish each 3 ft section with one light, straight pass.

wetedge.cap: Finish a whole wall corner to corner without a break, so the edges always overlap paint that's still wet.

Score the edge first</text><text x="10" y="176">with a sharp utility knife.</text>
tape.cap: Pull tape when the last coat is dry to the touch, within a few hours. Waiting days makes paint peel with it.

nap.cap: Longer nap holds more paint and reaches into bumps, but leaves more texture on a smooth wall.

caulk.cap: Caulk fills the line where trim meets wall so paint looks crisp. Gaps over 1/4" need a foam backer rod first.

lead.cap: Use an EPA-recognized kit and test each painted surface you'll sand, especially windows, doors and trim.

glossary: Cutting in
Brushing a band of paint along edges and corners where a roller can't reach.
Sheen
How shiny dried paint is: flat, eggshell, satin, semi-gloss, gloss.
Nap
The length of a roller cover's fibers.
Wet edge
Paint that's still wet at the edge of the area you've painted, so the next section blends in.
Lap mark
A darker stripe where wet paint was rolled over paint that had started to dry.
Boxing paint
Mixing several cans of the same color together so the color is even.
Primer
A first coat that seals and helps paint stick and cover.
TSP substitute
A wall cleaner that removes grease without the phosphates of old TSP.
Tipping off
A final light brush stroke along the length of the piece to level marks.
Recoat time
How long the can says to wait before the next coat.
Feathering
Thinning the edges of paint or filler so no ridge shows.
